content: A norm-referenced test is a type of assessment in which an individual's performance is compared to a representative sample of their peers, known as a normative sample. The process of comparing one test-taker to their peers is referred to as normative assessment. In contrast to norm-referenced testing, ipsative tests compare an individual's performance to their own previous performance over time. Criterion-referenced tests, on the other hand, evaluate an individual's performance against a predetermined standard or benchmark, translating the test score into a statement about the expected behavior or competency of someone with that score. The same test can sometimes be used in both norm-referenced and criterion-referenced ways. The terms norm-referenced test and criterion-referenced test were originally coined by Robert Glaser. Standards-based education reform is built on the principle that public education should define what every student should know and be able to do. Students are assessed against fixed benchmarks rather than being compared to one another or distributed along a bell curve. By requiring all students to meet these higher standards, education officials aim to ensure that every student earns a diploma that prepares them for success in the 21st century. Most state achievement tests are criterion-referenced, meaning they measure whether students meet a predetermined level of acceptable performance. Students either pass or fail based on whether they achieve this level. In contrast, norm-referenced tests set goals for students based on the average performance of their peers. Many college entrance exams and nationally administered school tests, such as the SAT, GRE, and Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC), are norm-referenced. These tests compare an individual's performance to that of a normative sample, often expressed as a percentile rank. Test-takers cannot fail a norm-referenced test; instead, their scores indicate how they performed relative to others who took the test. This approach is particularly useful when acceptable scores vary widely, as is the case for different colleges. For example, the average SAT score for Harvard University is estimated to be 2200 out of 2400, while the average for Indiana University is 1650. In contrast, nearly two-thirds of U.S. high school students are required to pass a criterion-referenced high school graduation exam. These exams set a fixed passing score, often aligned with university admission standards, regardless of whether the student intends to pursue higher education. Each state administers its own test and determines its own passing criteria. For instance, states like Massachusetts report high pass rates, while in Washington State, even average students and up to 80% of some minority groups fail. Critics, such as Alfie Kohn, argue that this practice is unfair to groups and individuals who do not perform as well as others. One disadvantage of norm-referenced tests is that they cannot measure the overall progress of a population, only the relative performance of individuals within that population. Criterion-referenced tests, by contrast, are better suited for evaluating the success of educational reform programs aimed at raising achievement levels for all students against new standards. These standards often assess skills beyond simple multiple-choice questions. However, in practice, the bar for passing is sometimes adjusted in response to high failure rates, and improvements may occur simply due to familiarity with the test or teaching to the test. Traditionally, grade levels in norm-referenced tests were determined by the middle 50% of scores. However, organizations like the National Children's Reading Foundation advocate for ensuring that nearly all children read at or above grade level by third grade—a goal that cannot be achieved using a norm-referenced definition of grade level. Critics of criterion-referenced tests point out that judges often set benchmarks around test items of varying difficulty without considering whether the items align with grade-level content standards or are developmentally appropriate. For example, the original 1997 sample problems for the Washington Assessment of Student Learning (WASL) 4th-grade mathematics test included items that were challenging for college-educated adults or solvable only with 10th-grade methods, such as similar triangles. The difficulty of test items and the cut-scores for passing levels often change from year to year, and pass rates can vary significantly between different grade levels. One criticism of the No Child Left Behind Act is that each state can design its own test, making it impossible to compare results across states. A RAND study of Kentucky's results found evidence of artificially inflated pass rates that were not reflected in improved scores on other tests, such as the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) or the SAT, administered to the same student populations during the same period. Graduation test standards are typically set at a level consistent with native-born four-year university applicants. However, this creates challenges for immigrant students with strong math skills but limited English proficiency, as high school graduation tests often require passing all sections, including language. For example, institutions like the University of Washington may admit strong Asian American or Latino students who fail the writing portion of the state WASL test, but these students would not receive a diploma under the testing requirement. Although tests like the WASL are intended as a minimal bar for high school, 27% of 10th graders applying for Washington State's Running Start program failed the math portion of the WASL. These students, who sought to take college-level courses in high school, often performed at a much higher level than average students. The same study concluded that the difficulty of the WASL was comparable to or greater than that of tests designed to place students already admitted to college. Norm-referenced tests avoid many of these issues because they do not impose expectations about what all students should know or be able to do. Instead, they reflect the actual performance levels of students without attempting to redesign the system to eliminate inequities. Goals for student performance are not raised annually until all students are proficient, and scores are not required to show continuous improvement under Total Quality Management systems. A rank-based system provides data on which students perform at an average level, which do better, and which do worse. This approach contrasts with the belief, often underlying standards-based systems, that all students can achieve uniformly high performance if sufficient incentives and penalties are applied. This fundamental difference in philosophy underpins the most significant distinctions between traditional and standards-based education systems.
